channel.title: Daily Recap — 🧠 AI
channel.description: What happened in 🧠 AI, recapped daily from subscribed feeds.

item.title: Meta's first frontier model, Muse Wonder, cracks the top tier
item.description:
Meta released its first frontier model family, Muse Wonder, and it's an instant contender: the top Wonder Full variant ranks in the top three on six of ten major benchmarks, with its biggest gains in agentic tasks. The catch is cost — cost per task has nearly tripled versus the previous generation, a reminder that raw capability still comes at a price.

The release comes with fresh context from a lengthy Q&A between Mark Zuckerberg and Alexandr Wang on the Muse app, where they discuss the risks of committing $100B+ to AI infrastructure, the reboot of Meta's AI team, and a push into agentic commerce. Meta is officially playing to win the frontier race now, not just open-weight it.

Sources

  • The Decoder: Meta's new frontier model Muse Wonder Full breaks into the AI top tier
  • TechCrunch: Meta releases its first frontier model, Muse Wonder
  • The Verge: Meta has some Wonder Full new AI models

item.title: OpenAI fires three safety researchers
item.description:
Three OpenAI safety researchers — Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, and Jasmine Wang — were fired, ostensibly for "mishandling sensitive company information." The firings are the latest in a string of safety-team departures and are likely to intensify scrutiny of how much priority OpenAI still places on alignment work.

The news landed the same day as a study in Science reporting that Google DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus has solved dozens of open math problems — including nine Erdős problems, two unsolved for 56 years — and survived peer review. Progress on capability and safety continue to tell very different stories.

Sources

  • The Zvi: OpenAI Fires Three Safety Researchers
  • The Decoder: Google Deepmind's AlphaProof Nexus solved dozens of open math problems and actually got peer reviewed

item.title: Microsoft to scale its own Maia AI chips to gigawatt levels by 2027
item.description:
Microsoft plans to make its in-house Azure Maia chips the main AI inference system across its products starting in 2027, deploying them at multi-gigawatt scale. The upcoming Maia 300 is said to deliver roughly 40 percent more performance per watt, a direct bid to cut dependence on Nvidia.

On the infrastructure front, NTT Data is reportedly in advanced talks to build an up to 500 MW data center for Anthropic in Osaka — among Japan's largest — at a potential cost of $6.3B. The AI buildout shows no sign of slowing, just new suppliers and new geographies.

Sources

  • The Decoder: Microsoft plans to scale its own Maia AI chips to gigawatt levels by 2027
  • Techmeme: Sources: NTT Data is in advanced talks to build an up to 500 MW data center for Anthropic in Osaka, among Japan's largest, potentially costing $6.3B (Nikkei Asia)

item.title: White House restores UK AI Safety Institute's access to frontier models
item.description:
The White House reversed course and restored the UK AI Safety Institute's early access to frontier models from Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and OpenAI. The Trump administration had cut off that access in September, and the restoration removes a point of friction in US-UK AI coordination.

Separately, Microsoft's president argued the UK is best placed to drive global AI regulation — a convenient position for a company courting London, but also a sign that the fight over who writes the AI rulebook is moving to new venues.

Sources

  • The Decoder: White House reverses course and restores UK AI Safety Institute's access to frontier models
  • TechCrunch: Microsoft president says UK is best placed to drive AI regulation

item.title: Anthropic claims big win against model distillation attacks — and warns small models may self-replicate
item.description:
Anthropic says new measures, including preserved thinking in Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, have reduced data harvesting through distillation attacks by roughly 90 to 99 percent — a meaningful defensive claim if it holds up.

In the same breath, Anthropic researchers warned that small AI models may be only months away from being able to self-replicate onto IoT devices like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes. It's a startling projection of how cheap self-proliferation is becoming, and it reframes the security conversation from datacenters to your living room.

Sources

  • Techmeme: Anthropic says new measures like preserved thinking in Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 have reduced data harvesting through distillation attacks by about 90% to 99% (Anthropic)
  • Techmeme: Anthropic researchers say small AI models may be months away from being able to self-replicate on IoT devices like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes (Anthropic)

item.title: Karpathy: the public has only seen the preview; Sakana's self-improving model hits a wall
item.description:
Anthropic's Andrej Karpathy argued the outside world has only seen "the preview" of what AI can actually do: roughly 5,000 people sit at the cutting edge while about 75 percent of humanity has barely touched LLMs. His point is about a widening knowledge gap as much as a capability gap.

Meanwhile, Sakana AI's MASS method — where a language model improves itself by solving tasks, judging results, and refining workflows — reached nearly a 70 percent win rate against its base model after two rounds, but couldn't fix its own blind spots. Self-improvement works, but the ceiling looks real.

Sources

  • The Decoder: Anthropic's Andrej Karpathy says "the external world has seen the preview" of what AI can actually do
  • The Decoder: Sakana AI's self-improving model gets better at solving and judging, but can't catch its own blind spots

item.title: Gary Marcus: is this the frontier labs' WeWork moment?
item.description:
Gary Marcus sees "ominous signs" that the big AI labs may be heading for their WeWork moment — overpromised returns, spiraling valuations, and a business model that doesn't pencil out. He doesn't predict a specific crash, but the argument is that the current funding frenzy has the familiar shape of an asset bubble.

The skepticism is worth pairing with today's market reality: JPMorgan and Goldman are leading a $5B loan sale for AI startup Volta at a yield of around 11 percent, and took the unusual step of underwriting just $1.3B of it to limit their own exposure. The credit markets are already pricing in doubt.

Sources

  • Marcus on AI: Could this be the Frontier Labs’ WeWork moment?
  • Techmeme: Sources: JPMorgan and Goldman, leading a $5B loan sale with a yield of ~11% for AI startup Volta, took a rare move to limit exposure by underwriting just $1.3B (Claire Ruckin/Bloomberg)

item.title: TypeSafe/Jev rockets past $100M ARR at a $7.5B valuation, three weeks after launch
item.description:
Latent.Space reports that TypeSafe/Jev has crossed $100M in annual recurring revenue just three weeks after launching, raising at a $7.5B valuation.

It's one of the fastest early ramps the AI coding-tools market has ever seen — and a sign that investors are still willing to pay up for developer-facing AI products with genuine traction, even this late in the cycle. The question now is whether the growth curve bends or breaks.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] TypeSafe/Jev at >$100M ARR, $7.5B valuation 3 weeks after launch

item.title: What industrial robotics can teach AI builders about reliable execution
item.description:
Latent.Space looks at industrial robotics for lessons on dependable AI execution in the real world. The core argument: reliability comes from tight feedback loops, constrained operating environments, and designing for failure from the start.

It's a useful corrective for agent developers moving from demos to production — the robotics industry already learned these lessons the hard way, over decades, with physical consequences for getting it wrong.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: Building AI for Reliable Execution: Lessons From Industrial Robotics

item.title: Simon Willison: Dwarf Fortress gets version control; Python 3.15 lands
item.description:
Simon Willison notes that Dwarf Fortress — the famously intricate simulation game — now uses version control, a fun intersection of game development and software craft from a project old enough to predate modern tooling norms.

He also flags Python 3.15.0's arrival in the actions/python-versions repo — worth knowing if you pin CI images and want to stay current.

Sources

  • Simon Willison: Dwarf Fortress uses version control now
  • Simon Willison: Python 3.15.0 added to actions/python-versions
